tardar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish tardar, from Latin tardāre.

pensar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish pensar, from Latin pēnsāre (possibly semi-learned in this form). Doublet of pesar. Compare English pensive.

cabeza.e: Inherited from Old Spanish cabeça, from Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural (reanalyzed as a feminine singular) of Latin capitium, diminutive of caput.

pena.e: Inherited from Old Spanish pena, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).

voz.e: Inherited from Old Spanish voz, from Latin vōcem. Sense 2 is presumably a semantic loan from Latin.

dolor.e: Inherited from Old Spanish dolor, from Latin dolor (“pain”).

salvo.e: Inherited from Latin salvus. Cognate with English safe.

salvar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish salvar, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus. Compare French sauver, Italian salvare.

sol.e: Inherited from Latin sōl (“sun”). The Peruvian currency makes reference to the meaning "sun", but is a shortening from Latin solidus.

soledad.e: Inherited from Latin sōlitātem. Doublet of saudade, which was borrowed from Portuguese.

tonto.e: Uncertain. Latin attonitus has been proposed, but there are phonological difficulties, namely unexpected loss of initial /a/ and lack of diphthongization; cf. the expected outcome atuendo.

hambre.e: Inherited from Old Spanish fambre, fanbre, famne (whence also Ladino ambre), from Vulgar Latin *faminem (the accusative of a nominative *famen or *famis), variant of Latin famēs, see there for more.

traje.e: Borrowed from Portuguese traje. Compare English train (“the long back section of a gown that is drawn along the floor”).

siete.e: Inherited from Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá), Italian sette, French sept, Portuguese sete, Old English seofon (English seven).

placer.e: Inherited from Latin placēre, with irregular conservation of initial /pl-/ (the expected form would be *llacer). Compare Portuguese prazer.

blanco.e: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“white, bright, blinding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bhleg- (“to shine”). Found as early as the Cantar de Mio Cid.

servicio.e: Borrowed from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, French service, Norman sèrvice).

muchacho.e: From older mochacho, from mozo + -acho. Cognate to Portuguese moçaço.

ley.e: Inherited from Old Spanish ley, from Latin lēgem (whence English legal and legitimate), from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s, from *leǵ- (“to gather”).

programa.e: Borrowed from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

carrera.e: Inherited from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Cognate with English career.

cumpleaños.e: Verb-object compound, composed of cumple (“to fulfill”) + años (“years”), literally “year-fulfiller”; an event celebrating the completion of a number of years of one’s life.

culo.e: Inherited from Old Spanish culo, from Latin culus.

canción.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin cantiōnem f (accusative singular), modified from the original Old Spanish cançón f, which was directly inherited, based on -ción.

hermoso.e: From Old Spanish fermoso, from Latin fōrmōsus.

universidad.e: Inherited from Old Spanish universidat, borrowed from Medieval Latin universitātem. By surface analysis, universo + -idad.

boda.e: Inherited from Latin vōta (“vows”), plural of vōtum.

sala.e: From a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, see also German Saal, Middle Low German seli, Old High German sal, from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”).

sal.e: Inherited from Old Spanish sal, from Latin salem (compare Catalan sal f, French sel m, Italian sale m, Portuguese sal m, Romanian sare f; also English salt). It is not known how the noun became feminine.

prisa.e: From Old Spanish priesa, from Latin pressa. Cognate with Sicilian prexa ~prescia.

suelo.e: Inherited from Old Spanish suelo, from Latin solum (“floor; ground, soil”).

cárcel.e: Inherited from Old Spanish carcel, from Latin carcerem. The feminine gender is analogous.

gobernar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish gobernar, gouernar, from Latin gubernāre, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer”).

prometer.e: Inherited from Old Spanish prometer, from Latin prōmittere (“to promise; to send forth”).

terrible.e: Borrowed from Latin terribilis. Cognate with English terrible.

regalo.e: Likely from French régal (“treat”), from Old French galer (“to enjoy oneself”), which English gala also derives from.

regalar.e: Disputed but likely from French régaler (“to treat, to cook well”), from régal (“treat”), from Old French galer (“to enjoy oneself”), from which English gala also is derived. Compare English regale.

dulce.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin dulcem (“sweet”). Also found in Old Spanish with the forms duz, duce (compare Portuguese doce). Cognate with English dulcet.

jurar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish iurar, from Latin iūrāre. Cognate with English jury.

ejército.e: Inherited from Old Spanish exército, borrowed from Latin exercitus.

fuente.e: Inherited from Old Spanish fuente, fuent, fuant, from Latin fontem m, from Proto-Indo-European.

tercero.e: Inherited from Latin tertiārius, from tertius. Doublet of terciario, a borrowing from the same source.

antiguo.e: Inherited from Old Spanish antigo, from Latin antīquus (variant form antīcus). The form antiguo in Spanish was probably the result of influence from the feminine form antigua on the older antigo.

genio.e: Borrowed from Latin genius, related to gignō (“to beget”) and genus (“birth, origin”).

recuperar.e: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre, from earlier reciperāre. Doublet of recobrar, which was inherited.

lengua.e: Inherited from Old Spanish lengua, from Latin lingua. Cognate with English tongue and language.

ladrón.e: Inherited from Old Spanish ladron, from Latin latrōnem. Cognate with Ladino ladrón.

examen.e: Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Compare the inherited doublet enjambre.

archivo.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).

girar.e: From Latin gȳrāre, from Latin gȳrus (“circle”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros). Doublet of yirar. Compare with French gyrer, Galician xirar, Portuguese girar, Italian girare. Compare also English gyrate, English gyro.

social.e: From Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion, companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, ally”).

comunidad.e: Borrowed from Latin commūnitātem, equivalent to común + -idad.

cero.e: Borrowed from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Andalusian Arabic صِفْر (ṣífr), from Classical Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, nothing, empty, void”).

pieza.e: Inherited from Old Spanish pieça, from Late Latin pettia, from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis. Compare French pièce, Italian pezza, Catalan and Portuguese peça.

estómago.e: Inherited from Old Spanish estomago (“maw”), from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos, “gullet; stomach”), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

legal.e: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis, from lēx (“law”). Doublet of leal.

california.e: First attested in Montalvo's Las sergas de Esplandián as the name of Calafia's monarchy. A name invented by the author to remind Spanish readers of the recent Reconquista, probably based on califa (“caliph”).

reino.e: From Old Spanish reino~regno, borrowed from Latin rēgnum. Compare English reign.

barrio.e: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy, “exterior”), referring to the outer, surrounding or less civilized or urbanized parts of a city, from classical Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy, “wild”).

granja.e: Inherited from Old Spanish granja (“barn”), from Old French grange, Vulgar Latin *grānica (“grain storage barn, granary; grange, small farm”), from Latin grānum (“grain”) from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.

esfuerzo.e: Inherited from Old Spanish esfuerço, equivalent to a modern esforzar + -o. The Old Spanish etymon is similarly derived from esforçar, from a Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, from *fortiāre, from fortia (“heroic actions”).

tesoro.e: Inherited from Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”).

empleo.e: Deverbal from emplear. Akin to French emploi, Italian impiego, and Occitan emplec.

emplear.e: Borrowed from Old French empleiier, variant of emploiier (compare modern French employer), from Latin implicāre. Doublet of implicar, borrowed directly from Latin. Cf.

clave.e: Borrowed from Latin clāvis (“key”). Compare the inherited doublet llave.

clavar.e: From clavo or from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus. Compare Portuguese cravar.

bolso.e: From bolsa. Compare English purse and burse.

respirar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish respirar, from Latin respīrāre. Cognate with English respire.

planta.e: Inherited from Old Spanish planta (“plant”), borrowed from Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”). Compare the now obsolete inherited form llanta.

compromiso.e: From Latin comprōmissum. Cognate with Catalan compromís, French compromis, Italian compromesso, Portuguese compromisso.

asegurar.e: Inherited from Old Spanish assegurar, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrare, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”). Compare English assure.

ira.e: From Latin īra. Cognate with English ire.

promesa.e: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prōmissa (“promise”) (attested in Medieval Latin per Du Cange), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

milagro.e: Inherited from Old Spanish miraglo, miráclo (after metathesis), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin mīrāculum. Compare Galician and Portuguese milagre.

soportar.e: Borrowed from Latin supportāre. First attested in the fifteenth century. Cognate with English support although divergent in meaning.

homicidio.e: Inherited from Old Spanish omicidio, omizidio, homicidio, homizidio, homiçidio, omeçidio, borrowed from Latin homicīdium. It replaced the inherited variant omezillo, omecillo in Old Spanish.

madera.e: Inherited from Old Spanish madera, from Latin māteria (compare French matière, Italian materia, Portuguese madeira), from māter (“source”, literally “mother”). Doublet of materia.

grado.e: Inherited from Old Spanish grado (“staircase; rank, dignity”), inherited from Latin gradus (“a step, pace; step of a staircase; degree”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).

lord.e: Borrowed from English lord, from Middle English lord; see lord for more.

milla.e: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin mīlia (“Roman mile”), plural of mīlle (“thousand”) in reference to its composition of a thousand Roman paces. In reference to the English unit, calqued from English mile.

escalera.e: Inherited from Old Spanish escalera, from Late Latin scālāria, from Latin scālae (“steps”). Compare English escalator, Asturian escalera, and Portuguese escaleira.

salvaje.e: First attested 1335; borrowed from Old Catalan and Occitan or Old Occitan salvatge, sauvatge, from Vulgar Latin salvāticus, alteration of Latin silvāticus (“wild”, literally “of the woods”), from silva (“forest, grove”).

traducción.e: Borrowed from Latin trāductiōnem (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).

ático.e: Borrowed from Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).

senior.e: Borrowed from Latin senior. Doublet of señor.

consumidor.e: Etymology tree Spanish consumir Proto-Indo-European *-tōr Proto-Italic *-tōr Latin -tor Spanish -dor Spanish consumidor From consumir + -dor.

nublado.e: From the past participle of nublar. Compare Asturian nubláu, Galician nubrado, Italian nuvolato, Portuguese nublado.

soprano.e: Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of soberano.

ares.e: Borrowed from Latin Arēs, from Ancient Greek Ἄρης (Árēs).

rehacer.e: Etymology tree Spanish re- Old Spanish fazer Spanish hacer Spanish rehacer From re- + hacer.

gómez.e: From a Visigothic personal name based on Gothic 𐌲𐌿𐌼𐌰 (guma, “man”) + -ez, literally “son of the man”, or from Gomi, a name attested in Nodicia de Kesos of unknown origin. Cognate to Portuguese Gomes.

gallinero.e: Inherited from Latin gallīnārium, from gallīna. Compare Portuguese galinheiro, Italian gallinaio.

recitar.e: Borrowed from Latin recitāre (cultism). Compare the inherited doublet rezar.
